case_study_insert.main_stem: Crestvale Retail Fashion (CRF) is a private limited company in the online fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2014 by Imogen Crestvale, the business sells trend-led clothing and accessories through its own e-commerce website and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. CRF plans to invest $720,000 in an automated e-commerce fulfilment and returns-processing centre, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $195,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.50 a unit and a selling price of $15.00, and currently produces 72,000 units a year. CRF faces two operational problems: its online return rate has reached 12.4% of orders and labour turnover in the packing team is rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: E-commerce and Quality Report â€” Q3 2025: The online store fulfilled 18,400 orders in the quarter, with 12.4% of orders returned and a defect rate of 2.2% on dispatched garments. Customer complaints fell from 46 to 27 per month. Median delivery time is 2.8 days. A survey of 750 online shoppers found that 61% would pay up to $0.60 more for a hassle-free returns service, and 58% check a retailer's sustainability policy before ordering. A training audit shows 18 of 64 packing staff have not completed induction on the new returns scanner; a short e-learning module costs $75 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $13.55 to $14.35 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills across retail and warehousing. (3) Wholesale textile and fabric costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, consumer spending on online fashion grew 2.6%, and retail inflation is running at 6.4%.

questions.question_text: CRF plans to fund part of its $720,000 expansion with a $420,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for CRF of using $300,000 retained profit to fund the expansion instead.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs CRF nothing in interest or capital repayments, so the $300,000 finances an automated e-commerce fulfilment and returns-processing centre without increasing the $420,000 debt commitment. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 9.8% rise in textile and fabric input costs named in Appendix 3, protecting the $6.50 contribution per unit earned on each of the 72,000 units sold.

Point 2: Retaining profit leaves ownership and control with Imogen Crestvale and the existing owners, so no bank can impose conditions on how the $720,000 investment is run. It is also flexible: with 64 staff and a democratic leadership style, CRF can time spending on the new facility to match cash generation. A bank loan would require regular interest and eventual repayment, which would strain cash flow if online fashion retail demand weakened during the expansion.

Taken together, the $300,000 funds an automated e-commerce fulfilment and returns-processing centre without competing with the $420,000 debt service, leaving the $195,000 of annual fixed costs to be covered by the $6.50 contribution on each of the 72,000 units. In online fashion retail, where the 9.8% input-cost rise already pressures margins, avoiding compulsory interest payments gives CRF a materially safer route than increasing its borrowings for a flat organisation with 64 staff.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to Crestvale Retail Fashion and its financing choice.

questions.question_text: CRF is promoting its online fashion retail offering. Consider national social media advertising, fashion influencer partnerships, or pay-per-click search advertising. Which should CRF choose to promote its e-commerce brand? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National social media advertising: Paid social campaigns can reach large numbers of fashion shoppers nationally and can target by interest, building awareness of the online fashion retail brand quickly. However, cost per click rises with competition, and much of the reach will be people who never buy online knitwear or garments, so spend can be wasteful for a business funding a $720,000 expansion.

Fashion influencer partnerships: Influencers showcase the clothing on real customers and can drive traffic to the website, consistent with the $0.60% of surveyed shoppers who act on reviews and recommendations. Credibility is high and cost is variable, but results depend on the influencer's reputation and are hard to control; a poor fit could damage the brand built by Imogen Crestvale.

Pay-per-click search advertising: Search ads intercept shoppers at the moment they look for fashion items, giving measurable, intent-led traffic to the e-commerce site. The downside is that popular keywords are expensive and traffic stops the moment spending stops, so it does not build lasting brand equity for CRF.

Recommendation: CRF should choose fashion influencer partnerships. They reach the precise fashion-aware segment identified in the survey, are far cheaper than broad social media campaigns, and create content that keeps selling after the initial post. National social advertising is rejected as too expensive and untargeted, while pay-per-click search is rejected because it buys only short-term, intent-led traffic and builds no lasting brand for a business investing $720,000 in a fulfilment centre.

With fixed costs of $195,000 a year and a $420,000 loan to service, CRF needs volume at a controlled cost, so the chosen method must reach buyers who will actually convert; that is why the two rejected options, despite their superficial appeal, are set aside in favour of the more targeted approach. The decision should be reviewed against the sales and enquiry figures in Appendix 1 after one campaign cycle, and the spend justified only if the extra orders cover the $6.50 contribution needed toward the $195,000 fixed costs of the online fashion retail business.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of promotional methods with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of the business with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of Crestvale Retail Fashion with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the two rejected options lose.

questions.question_text: CRF's labour turnover in the packing team is rising. Explain two benefits for CRF of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in that team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 64 packing staff a voice in how the new returns scanner is introduced, so they are more likely to accept the change and feel valued. Higher job satisfaction should reduce the rising labour turnover and the 8.5%-style absence pressure in the team, keeping experienced staff who can process the 12.4% of orders that are returned efficiently.

Point 2: Involving packers in decisions generates practical ideas about returns handling from the people doing the job, improving service and reducing complaints that have fallen only from 46 to 27 a month. Because the structure is flat and leadership is democratic, suggestions travel quickly to Imogen Crestvale, raising commitment and helping the $720,000 returns centre bed in without disrupting 72,000-unit output.

These benefits matter because fixed costs of $195,000 mean CRF must keep output close to 72,000 units a year; every experienced worker lost through turnover or absence is replaced at a retraining cost shown in Appendix 1, and a destabilised team would slow the $720,000 rollout. Better motivation therefore protects the quality figures reported in Appendix 1 and the $6.50 contribution on each unit, which is what allows the private limited company to absorb the 9.8% rise in textile and fabric costs without cutting the 72,000-unit plan.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to Crestvale Retail Fashion's problem, costs and output.

questions.question_text: CRF must train staff to use its new equipment. Consider on-the-job induction on the new returns scanner or external e-learning modules at $75 per employee. Which should CRF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job induction on the returns scanner: Training at the returns desk is specific to CRF's own scanner and process, costs no external fee, and keeps the 18 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 72,000-unit output and the effort to cut the 12.4% return rate. However, peer trainers are themselves packing staff, so their work may suffer and bad habits can spread; there is also no formal certificate for the $720,000 centre.

External e-learning at $75 per employee: Structured modules give consistent content and a record of completion for all 18 staff, costing 18 Ã— $75 = $1,350 in total, small against the $720,000 investment. The course can be taken flexibly, but generic content may not match the new scanner exactly and time spent training reduces short-term packing capacity.

Decision: CRF should choose on-the-job induction first, backed by short e-learning modules for the 18 staff. On-the-job training is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids output loss while labour turnover is a problem; full e-learning alone is rejected because it is generic and cannot teach the exact returns process that the $720,000 hub depends on.

The wider context reinforces this decision. With fixed costs of $195,000 and the $420,000 loan to service, CRF cannot afford the output loss that follows withdrawing the staff concerned from the line for long. The documented problem in Appendix 1 â€” the defect and turnover figures â€” makes early practical competence on the actual equipment more valuable than a generic certificate. A short external top-up later can add formal recognition without the disruption of full off-the-job training, so the chosen blend protects both the 72,000-unit volume and the quality the private limited company is trying to improve as it invests $720,000 in new online fashion retail capacity.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to the business.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of the business.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of Crestvale Retail Fashion with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CRF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs Ã· Contribution per unit. Substitution: $195,000 Ã· ($15.00 âˆ’ $8.50) = $195,000 Ã· $6.50 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price âˆ’ Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $15.00 âˆ’ $8.50 = $6.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CRF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 72,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 42,000 units, to judge whether the $720,000 investment is safely profitable.
2. Contribution per unit of $6.50 lets managers model a discount: for example a 5% cut in the $15.00 selling price would lower contribution and show the extra volume needed to cover $195,000 fixed costs.
3. With $195,000 fixed costs and $6.50 contribution, managers can set the sales volumes needed to service the $420,000 loan before committing further capital to an automated e-commerce fulfilment and returns-processing centre.
4. Unit cost of about $11.21 ($195,000 Ã· 72,000 units + $8.50) can be benchmarked each quarter to spot waste from the textile and fabric cost inflation of 9.8% and to check whether the $8.50 variable cost can be renegotiated. Together these figures guide pricing, volume and cost control at CRF.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 42,000 units against 72,000 output; pricing/discount modelling against $195,000 fixed costs; loan-service volume for the $720,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at about $11.21 to tackle 9.8% input-cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CRF's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CRF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.27 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.42 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.64 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.68 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $95 inventories + $64 trade receivables + $32 cash = $191; 2025 current assets = $118 + $58 + $51 = $227. Dividing by current liabilities of $150 (2024) and $160 (2025) gives the 2024 figure of 1.27 and the 2025 figure of 1.42. For the second measure, (current assets âˆ’ inventories) Ã· current liabilities gives 2024: ($191 âˆ’ $95) Ã· $150 = $96 Ã· $150 = 0.64; 2025: ($227 âˆ’ $118) Ã· $160 = $109 Ã· $160 = 0.68.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. The 2024 coverage of 1.27 rose to 1.42 in 2025, meaning current assets cover short-term obligations more comfortably, helped by current liabilities falling from $150 to $160. The stricter measure, which excludes inventories, improved from 0.64 to 0.68, so CRF is less dependent on selling stock to meet debts â€” important while it services a $420,000 loan and funds a $720,000 expansion. Trade receivables moved from $64 to $58, tying up cash that could be slower to collect, and inventories moved from $95 to $118, so availability for peak demand should still be watched. Non-current assets grew from $1,120 to $1,600, consistent with the new investment, while capital employed rose from $1,350 to $1,720.

Conclusion: CRF's financial position has improved. Both short-term solvency measures rose (1.27 to 1.42 and 0.64 to 0.68) and the improvement does not rely on inventory alone. The main residual risk is the $58 of trade receivables, so tighter credit control is advisable before further expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether Crestvale Retail Fashion's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CRF of introducing a guaranteed hassle-free returns service priced $0.60 higher, as its survey suggested.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A hassle-free returns service priced $0.60 higher matches the 61% of surveyed shoppers who said they would pay more for it, so it can raise revenue and strengthen loyalty at a time when the return rate is 12.4% of orders. It also differentiates the e-commerce brand from rivals.

Disadvantage: Handling more returns adds cost to processing and refunds, which could push up the $8.50 variable cost per unit and erode the $6.50 contribution. If the 9.8% rise in textile costs also lifts prices, the premium may not be accepted by all customers, reducing demand for the 72,000 units.

Managers should set the premium against the $6.50 contribution per unit and the $195,000 annual fixed costs: the survey evidence in Appendix 1 suggests customers will pay more, but the 9.8% rise in textile and fabric costs and the need to sustain 72,000 units mean the net gain must be checked. If volumes fall, the extra cost would not be recovered, so the effect should be reviewed after one quarter. For a private limited company with 64 staff, the change also affects training and the brand Imogen Crestvale has built, so it belongs alongside the service and quality improvements already reported in Appendix 1 rather than being introduced in isolation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to Crestvale Retail Fashion's data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.0%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in textile and fabric input costs will affect CRF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): The insert states CRF has a $420,000 ten-year bank loan. A rise of 0.75 percentage points adds 0.75% Ã— $420,000 = $3,150 a year if the loan is variable-rate; if the rate is fixed, the direct effect is nil. Higher base rates could also raise the cost of future borrowing for the $720,000 expansion and make consumers more cautious about online fashion retail spending.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $14.35 per hour): With a workforce of 64, this raises wage costs in the partly hourly-paid fulfilment and store roles. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so no defensible annual wage bill can be invented. The only honest yardstick is the productivity already derivable: 72,000 units Ã· 64 staff = 1,125 units per worker. A wage rise is absorbable only if productivity holds near that level or output grows, otherwise unit labour costs rise and the $6.50 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input cost inflation (9.8% in textile and fabric): CRF's variable cost is $8.50 a unit and the insert does not decompose it, so the only defensible bound is to apply the full rise: 9.8% Ã— $8.50 = $0.833 a unit, which at 72,000 units is about $59,976.00 a year (72,000 Ã— $0.833). Even a smaller effect would cut the $6.50 contribution and threaten the $720,000 investment; the $58% premium from the survey can recover only part of it.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in textile and fabric costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 72,000 units sold, directly erodes the $6.50 contribution that justifies the $720,000 expansion, and is only partly offset by the premium. The interest rise is smaller ($3,150 at most, and possibly nil), and the wage impact, though unavoidable, can be managed through the 1,125-unit productivity the business already achieves.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of Crestvale Retail Fashion with a well-justified judgment on which has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
